newsitem.title: USA: Plight of homeless U.S. veterans to get airing.
newsitem.headline: Plight of homeless U.S. veterans to get airing.

text.p: They wear rags. They huddle in doorways. They beg for quarters. They are homeless military veterans and they are everywhere in the United States.

And to discuss their plight, representatives of a national organisation are gathering in Washington Thursday through Saturday to try to help some 275,00 men and women who served in the U.S. military but now are down and out.
The goal of the group, the National Coalition for Homeless Veterans, is simple -- to put itself out of business by having no more veterans living on the streets.

The group's leaders say their goal is unlikely to be achieved, in the near future at least, but in the meantime some 90 representatives of the coalition representing homeless shelters, food kitchens, alcohol treatment centres and job counsellors plan to try to do something about former service people having hard times.
This will be the first national convention of the coalition founded in 1990 to give homeless veterans a voice in power centres in Congress and federal departments.
One of the speakers at the conference will be John Mulligan, 46, of San Francisco, a Scot but a U.S. Air Force veteran who spent two years in Vietnam in the war.
A few years after his discharge in 1974, Mulligan, who suffered from alcoholism, became homeless and lived under bridges and on the streets on and off for about 15 years.

In an interview with Reuters, Mulligan said he will tell the participants at the conference that "we've lost our compassion ... America has got to regain its compassion ...unless we help the helpless or those with no hope, there's not much future for the whole country."
He said he will urge people "to reach out to these people -- when you pass a homeless veteran in the street, don't kick him, give him a dollar."
Mulligan also said the Pentagon, Veterans Administration and other agencies should spend more money and interest in the problems of homeless veterans.
During his recovery from alcoholism Mulligan met an author who said he had writing talent.
Mulligan has just written a book, "Shopping Cart Soldiers," about his own plight that will be published this fall by Curbstone Press of Willimantic, Connecticut.
Despite his compassion for American homeless people, Mulligan is not naturalised but is a legal resident. "I'll be a Scot til I die," he said in a heavy brogue.
Mulligan was born in Kirkintilloch, Scotland, one of 10 children, and came to the United States in 1950 when his father, an electronics engineer, was transferred.
The homeless veterans group is armed with statistics showing the problem of homeless veterans to be extremely serious.
On any one night, spokeswoman Judith Speizer Crandell said in an interview, it is believed some 275,000 veterans are homeless, but she said there is no firm number.
Many suffer from alcoholism, drug abuse or post traumatic stress disorder -- with symptoms of depression, flashbacks and stress from war.
Homeless veterans represent an estimated one-third of the homeless in the nation, she said, although other estimates said the number is much higher.
About six out of 10 of the homeless veterans are from the Vietnam War era.

During meetings at the conference, representatives of various groups will gave discussions with officials of government agencies and congressional committees and the coalition hopes to frame a legislative agenda for next year.
